entries.body:
E90 is the sedan body code for the 2005-2011 BMW 3 Series generation. The same platform also covers the E91 Touring (wagon), E92 (coupe), and E93 (convertible).

Rear-wheel drive unless the car is badged xi, which means xDrive all-wheel drive. Front suspension is a double-pivot MacPherson strut design, rear is a multi-link axle.

The US-market 325i with the N52B25 engine was sold through roughly the 2006-2008 model years, before the LCI (facelift) update changed the front and rear lights, bumpers, and some interior trim.

Source: general public automotive reference knowledge. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, BMW made plenty of running changes within a single model year.

entries.body:
2.5L naturally aspirated inline-6, one of the first BMW engines built with a magnesium/aluminum composite block instead of all-aluminum or iron. Uses dual VANOS (variable valve timing) and Valvetronic (variable valve lift, which lets the engine run without a traditional throttle plate for most operating conditions).

Output is roughly 215-218 hp depending on market and model year.

Known wear points across the N52 family, not specific disasters, just things an owner this age should expect eventually:

- Electric water pump and plastic thermostat housing failures
- Plastic coolant pipes and expansion tank cracking with age and heat cycles
- VANOS solenoid issues causing rough idle or a check engine light
- Valve cover gasket seepage, usually shows up as a faint burning smell after the engine's been running a while

Source: general public automotive reference knowledge. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace a failed or failing alternator.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal first, this is a live electrical component.
2. Remove the serpentine belt (see the serpentine belt procedure).

### Removal
1. Disconnect the electrical connector and the B+ terminal nut from the alternator, note the orientation before you pull anything off.
2. Remove the alternator mounting bolts, these are typically one-time-use torque-to-yield bolts on this engine, buy new ones before you start, don't plan to reuse the old ones.
3. Maneuver the alternator out, it can be a tight fit depending on what else is routed through the engine bay on your specific car.

### Installation
1. Install the new or rebuilt alternator in reverse order, using new mounting bolts, torque them to spec in the correct stages.
2. Torque the B+ terminal nut to spec, reinstall the belt, reconnect the battery.
3. Start the engine and verify charging voltage is correct before considering the job done.
entries.torque_specs: Alternator mounting bolts: commonly cited as 10 Nm plus an additional 180 degree turn, consistent with a torque-to-yield, one-time-use aluminum bolt design, do not reuse these bolts. B+ terminal nut: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec. Confirm both against your exact year before relying on these numbers.
entries.part_numbers: Alternator, and the mounting bolts if they're the one-time-use type for your car: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Also confirm whether your alternator has an integrated voltage regulator before ordering a replacement, this varies.
entries.tools_needed: Socket set, torque wrench capable of angle-based tightening if your bolts use the torque-to-yield spec, possibly need to loosen other components for clearance depending on your engine bay layout.
entries.notes_warnings: Always disconnect the battery first. Double check the B+ terminal nut is properly torqued, a loose one can arc and melt the connector, which turns a straightforward job into an expensive one. If charging voltage still looks wrong after the swap, check the battery and wiring before assuming the new alternator is also bad, it's an easy trap to fall into.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, cross-checked against public forum discussion of the specific torque spec for this job. Not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the 12V battery. The important part most people miss on this generation of BMW isn't the physical swap, it's registering the new battery afterward.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Note your radio presets and any settings that might reset, some will be retained by the car's memory, some won't.
2. Locate the battery, on this generation it's commonly in the trunk rather than the engine bay, check under the trunk floor panel or side trim.

### Swap
1. Disconnect the negative terminal first, then the positive, remove any retaining clamp.
2. Remove the old battery, install the new one of the correct type and capacity, reconnect positive first, then negative.

### Registration (the step most people skip)
1. Register the new battery with the car's electrical system. This generation uses an Intelligent Battery Sensor (IBS) that tracks battery age and condition to manage charging behavior. If you don't register the replacement, the car keeps charging based on the old battery's profile, which noticeably shortens the life of the new one.
2. Registration is typically done either through the car's own iDrive/instrument cluster menu on later software versions, or via diagnostic software (commonly used tools in the community include INPA or similar BMW-specific diagnostic software), confirm what your specific car's software version supports before assuming the in-car menu option exists.
entries.torque_specs: Battery terminal clamps and tray retaining hardware: typically low torque, hand-tight-plus-a-bit is common guidance, verify against RealOEM or dealer spec if you want an exact number.
entries.part_numbers: Battery: confirm the correct capacity (Ah) and type (standard vs AGM) for your car before ordering, this varies by options package, not just by model, verify against RealOEM.com or your door-jamb sticker.
entries.tools_needed: Basic wrench set for the terminals, a battery registration tool or access to the car's menu system, a memory-saver device if you want to avoid losing radio/seat memory settings during the swap.
entries.difficulty: Easy (physical swap) to Medium (if registration requires diagnostic software you don't already have access to)
entries.time_estimate: 20-30 minutes for the physical swap, variable for registration depending on your tools
entries.notes_warnings: This is the step people skip and then wonder why their "new battery" is dead in eight months. If your battery lives in the trunk, also check that the battery vent tube (if equipped) is properly connected, venting matters for AGM batteries in an enclosed space. Disconnecting the battery on this generation can also trigger window/sunroof initialization issues afterward, worth knowing that one-touch window operation sometimes needs to be re-learned per window after a battery disconnect.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, and confirm what registration method your car's software actually supports before starting.

entries.summary: Replace brake pads and, when worn or scored past spec, the rotors, front or rear.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the wheel bolts slightly before jacking, then jack up the car and support it on stands, remove the wheel.

### Removal
1. Remove the caliper guide bolts (or the full caliper mounting bracket bolts if you're also replacing the rotor).
2. Lift the caliper off and support it with wire, never let it hang by the brake line, that stresses and can damage the hose.
3. Remove the old pads and anti-rattle clips/shims.
4. If replacing the rotor: remove the caliper bracket, then the rotor, which may be stuck on by corrosion, a few taps with a rubber mallet usually frees it.
5. Clean the hub face before installing a new rotor, debris here causes a wobble that feels like a warped rotor later.

### Installation
1. Compress the caliper piston back in with a proper tool, on the rear axle some BMWs use an electric parking brake caliper that needs to be wound back with a special tool or retracted electronically, do not just push it like a front piston.
2. Install new pads and clips, reinstall caliper and bracket, torque everything to spec.
3. Pump the brake pedal firmly several times before driving to seat the pads against the rotor.
entries.torque_specs: Caliper guide bolts: around 30 Nm. Caliper bracket-to-knuckle bolts: typically higher, in the 100+ Nm range. Wheel bolts: around 120 Nm. Verify all of these against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact axle and year, front and rear specs differ.
entries.part_numbers: Brake pads, rotors, and anti-rattle clip sets: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, front and rear are different part numbers and some years changed rotor diameter.
entries.tools_needed: Caliper piston compression tool (and the electric parking brake retraction tool/procedure if doing the rear), torque wrench, jack and stands.
entries.notes_warnings: Reset the brake pad wear sensor if your car has one, or the dashboard warning light stays on even with fresh pads. Bed in new pads with a series of gentle stops from moderate speed before relying on hard braking, this transfers an even layer of pad material onto the rotor and meaningfully affects how well they work afterward. If the rear uses an electric parking brake, do not attempt to compress that piston with a standard tool, you can damage the motor.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.procedure_name: Cabin and engine air filter change
entries.summary: Replace the cabin (pollen) filter and the engine intake air filter, two separate, unrelated filters often done together since both are quick.
entries.steps:
### Cabin filter
1. Open the glovebox, remove the side stops/dampers so the glovebox can swing down fully, or remove it entirely depending on your exact trim.
2. Locate the filter housing behind the glovebox, release the retaining clips or cover.
3. Slide the old filter out, noting the airflow direction arrow printed on the frame.
4. Install the new filter in the same orientation, close everything back up.

### Engine air filter
1. Locate the airbox, typically on the side of the engine bay near the front.
2. Release the clips or screws holding the airbox lid closed.
3. Lift the lid, remove the old filter, note its orientation.
4. Wipe out any debris sitting in the bottom of the airbox before installing the new filter.
5. Reinstall the lid and secure the clips/screws.
entries.torque_specs: No meaningful torque specs, these are clip and screw fasteners, hand-tight is correct for essentially all of them.
entries.part_numbers: Cabin filter and engine air filter: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, cabin filters especially have variants (with or without activated charcoal) depending on trim.
entries.tools_needed: None beyond basic hand tools, this is one of the easier jobs on the car.
entries.notes_warnings: Pay attention to the airflow direction arrow on the cabin filter, installing it backward reduces airflow and defeats some of the filtration. If the cabin filter housing has standing water or visible mold when you open it, check the cowl drain area for a clog, a blocked drain is a common cause and just replacing the filter won't fix the underlying issue.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Drain and replace the engine coolant as routine service, or because the system was opened for other work.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Let the engine cool completely before opening any part of the cooling system, this is genuinely dangerous hot.
2. Remove the engine undertray if present.

### Draining
1. Open the radiator drain petcock, or disconnect the lower radiator hose, into a drain pan. Loosen the expansion tank cap to help it drain faster.
2. Close the drain petcock or reconnect the hose once fully drained.

### Refilling and bleeding
1. Refill with BMW-spec coolant mixed to the correct ratio, never use a generic universal coolant, the wrong chemistry attacks the plastic components in this cooling system.
2. Bleed the system: this engine needs air purged properly through the bleed screw on the expansion tank or thermostat housing, or it will run hot and you'll think you have a different problem.
3. Run the engine to operating temperature with the heater on full blast, this helps push trapped air out. Check for leaks, then top off the level once the car has fully cooled.
entries.torque_specs: Hose clamps and any fasteners disturbed during the drain: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, these vary by exactly what you're touching.
entries.part_numbers: BMW-spec blue antifreeze, correct ratio for this generation: verify exact OEM part number against RealOEM.com using your VIN.
entries.tools_needed: Drain pan, BMW-spec coolant, a cooling system bleed/fill tool makes for a much cleaner bleed if you have access to one.
entries.notes_warnings: If you're already in here and the thermostat housing or water pump looks original, strongly consider replacing them proactively rather than coming back into the same job in a year. Both are known weak points on this engine family. Never skip the bleed step, trapped air is the most common reason a coolant change "doesn't fix" an overheating issue.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the plastic coolant expansion tank, a known weak point on this engine family, it cracks over time from repeated heat and pressure cycling, usually showing up as a slow coolant loss with no visible puddle.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Let the engine cool completely before opening any part of the cooling system.
2. Relieve system pressure by slowly loosening the expansion tank cap.
3. Drain coolant down below the level of the tank, you don't need to fully drain the whole system for this job, just enough that coolant isn't pouring out when the tank is disconnected.

### Removal
1. Disconnect the hoses from the tank, note which hose goes where, they're not always obviously different.
2. Disconnect the low coolant level sensor connector if your tank has one built in.
3. Remove the tank's mounting bolts or clips, lift it out.

### Installation and bleeding
1. Transfer the level sensor to the new tank if it's a separate part, or confirm the new tank includes one if that's how your car is equipped.
2. Install the new tank, reconnect hoses and the sensor, refill coolant to spec.
3. Bleed the system per the standard coolant bleed procedure, trapped air here causes the same overheating symptoms as a full coolant change done without bleeding.
entries.torque_specs: Mounting bolts and hose clamps: low torque, hand-tight-plus-a-quarter-turn is common guidance for the clamps, verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for the mounting hardware.
entries.part_numbers: Coolant expansion tank, and the low coolant level sensor if it's a separate part on your car: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Some aftermarket tanks are known to have the same cracking issue as the original design, worth checking owner discussion on whether a specific aftermarket brand has a better track record before you buy the cheapest option.
entries.tools_needed: Drain pan, basic hand tools, BMW-spec coolant to refill.
entries.notes_warnings: Inspect the hoses connecting to the tank while you're in there, if they're original and brittle, replacing them at the same time saves a second coolant drain and bleed later. Never use non-BMW-spec coolant, the wrong chemistry attacks the plastic components throughout this cooling system, which is part of why these plastic parts fail as often as they do.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the front lower control arms (often called thrust arms and tension struts on this chassis) or just their bushings. One of the most common wear items on an E9X, usually announced by a clunk over bumps and vague steering.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the wheel bolts, jack the car up, support it properly on stands, remove the front wheel.
2. Spray the control arm ball joint nuts and bushing bracket bolts with penetrating fluid and give it time to work, these live in the salt spray and seize readily.

### Removal
1. Remove the nut from the ball joint where the arm meets the steering knuckle.
2. Separate the ball joint with a proper ball joint separator, not by hammering the knuckle, you can damage the knuckle or the new part's boot.
3. Unbolt the bushing bracket from the subframe, note bolt positions and lengths before they come out.
4. Remove the arm. If you're only replacing bushings rather than the whole arm, press the old bushing out now, this needs a press or the right puller setup, it's not a hand-tool job.

### Installation
1. Fit the new arm or pressed-in bushing, hand-start all fasteners before torquing anything.
2. Torque the ball joint nut and bushing bracket bolts to spec.
3. Critically: final-torque the bushing bolts with the suspension at normal ride height, not hanging free on the jack. Torquing a rubber bushing at full droop preloads it permanently and it will tear early.
4. Reinstall the wheel, lower the car, and get a four-wheel alignment, this job changes the geometry.
entries.torque_specs: Ball joint nut and bushing bracket bolts: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, these are substantial fasteners and several are one-time-use torque-to-yield on this chassis, check before reusing any of them.
entries.part_numbers: Control arms, tension struts, and their bushings: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Left and right are often different part numbers, and some years changed the bushing design.
entries.tools_needed: Ball joint separator, torque wrench, penetrating fluid, jack and stands, and either a press or a bushing puller kit if you're doing bushings rather than complete arms.
entries.notes_warnings: Replacing complete arms rather than pressing bushings is more expensive in parts but far less painful in labor, worth pricing both ways before starting. Always get an alignment afterward, skipping it will eat a set of tires. If one side is worn, the other is usually not far behind, doing both at once saves repeating the whole teardown.

procedure front-control-arms procedures/front-control-arms.md front control arms and bushings e90 n52b25 suspension replace the front lower control arms (often called thrust arms and tension struts on this chassis) or just their bushings. one of the most common wear items on an e9x, usually announced by a clunk over bumps and vague steering. ### preparation
1. loosen the wheel bolts, jack the car up, support it properly on stands, remove the front wheel.
2. spray the control arm ball joint nuts and bushing bracket bolts with penetrating fluid and give it time to work, these live in the salt spray and seize readily.

### removal
1. remove the nut from the ball joint where the arm meets the steering knuckle.
2. separate the ball joint with a proper ball joint separator, not by hammering the knuckle, you can damage the knuckle or the new part's boot.
3. unbolt the bushing bracket from the subframe, note bolt positions and lengths before they come out.
4. remove the arm. if you're only replacing bushings rather than the whole arm, press the old bushing out now, this needs a press or the right puller setup, it's not a hand-tool job.

### installation
1. fit the new arm or pressed-in bushing, hand-start all fasteners before torquing anything.
2. torque the ball joint nut and bushing bracket bolts to spec.
3. critically: final-torque the bushing bolts with the suspension at normal ride height, not hanging free on the jack. torquing a rubber bushing at full droop preloads it permanently and it will tear early.
4. reinstall the wheel, lower the car, and get a four-wheel alignment, this job changes the geometry. ball joint nut and bushing bracket bolts: verify against realoem or dealer spec, these are substantial fasteners and several are one-time-use torque-to-yield on this chassis, check before reusing any of them. control arms, tension struts, and their bushings: verify exact oem part numbers against realoem.com using your vin. left and right are often different part numbers, and some years changed the bushing design. ball joint separator, torque wrench, penetrating fluid, jack and stands, and either a press or a bushing puller kit if you're doing bushings rather than complete arms. medium-hard 2-3 hours per side replacing complete arms rather than pressing bushings is more expensive in parts but far less painful in labor, worth pricing both ways before starting. always get an alignment afterward, skipping it will eat a set of tires. if one side is worn, the other is usually not far behind, doing both at once saves repeating the whole teardown. general public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the front struts (shock absorber inserts), usually together with the spring, strut mount, and bump stop as a complete assembly.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the wheel bolts, jack the car, support it on stands, remove the front wheel.
2. Before anything else: if you are reusing the original spring, you need a proper spring compressor. A compressed coil spring stores enough energy to kill someone. If you are not completely confident with a compressor, buy a pre-assembled complete strut assembly instead, it removes this hazard entirely.

### Removal
1. Disconnect anything mounted to the strut body: the sway bar end link, the ABS sensor wire, and the brake line bracket.
2. Support the control arm with a jack so the suspension doesn't drop when the strut comes free.
3. Remove the lower strut-to-knuckle pinch bolt or mounting bolts.
4. Open the hood and remove the upper strut mount nuts in the strut tower, support the strut from below so it doesn't fall as the last nut comes out.
5. Lower the assembly out.

### Installation
1. If reusing the spring, transfer it with the compressor and fit a new strut mount and bump stop, these wear out and it's false economy to reuse them.
2. Fit the assembly back up into the tower, start the upper nuts by hand.
3. Reconnect the lower mount, sway bar link, ABS wire, and brake line bracket.
4. Torque everything to spec, with the suspension loaded at ride height for anything that passes through a rubber bushing.
5. Reinstall the wheel, lower the car, get a four-wheel alignment.
entries.torque_specs: Upper strut mount nuts and lower strut-to-knuckle fasteners: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, several of these are one-time-use on this chassis. Wheel bolts: around 120 Nm.
entries.part_numbers: Struts, springs, strut mounts, and bump stops: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Spring rates differ between standard, sport, and xDrive setups, ordering the wrong spring changes ride height.
entries.tools_needed: Spring compressor (only if reusing springs), torque wrench, jack and stands, penetrating fluid.
entries.notes_warnings: This is the job where people get hurt. A spring compressor slipping under load is genuinely dangerous, so if there's any doubt, complete pre-assembled strut units cost more but remove the risk entirely. Always replace struts in pairs across an axle, a new strut on one side and a worn one on the other makes the car handle unpredictably. Alignment afterward is not optional.

entries.summary: Replace engine oil and the oil filter element as part of routine service.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Warm the engine for a few minutes so the oil flows freely, then shut it off.
2. Remove the engine undertray.

### Draining
1. Remove the drain plug and let the oil fully drain into a pan, this takes longer than people expect, don't rush it.
2. Remove the oil filter housing cap (large plastic cap near the front of the engine), replace the filter element and both O-rings on the cap.

### Refilling
1. Reinstall the drain plug with a new crush washer, and the filter cap.
2. Refill with the correct oil spec and quantity, start the engine, check for leaks around the drain plug and filter cap, then check the level once settled.
entries.torque_specs: Oil drain plug: around 25 Nm. Oil filter housing cap: around 25 Nm. Verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact year, these are commonly cited figures, not pulled from your specific car's documentation.
entries.part_numbers: Oil filter element and drain plug crush washer: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Oil spec: BMW Longlife-01 5W-30 is the commonly cited spec for this engine generation, capacity is roughly 6.5 liters with filter, confirm both against your owner's manual.
entries.tools_needed: Oil filter housing wrench (typically 36mm), drain pan, torque wrench.
entries.notes_warnings: Don't overtighten the filter housing cap, it's plastic and cracks easily, especially once it's a few years old. Let the oil drain fully before refilling, a partial drain leaves old oil and contaminants behind.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the oil filter housing itself, not just the filter element inside it. This is a different, bigger job than a routine oil change, done when the housing has cracked or is leaking from somewhere other than the cap O-rings.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Drain the oil first, same as for a routine oil change, there's no way to remove the housing with oil still in the system.
2. Remove whatever is in the way for access, on this engine that commonly includes intake ducting and sometimes the alternator or its bracket, depending on exactly how the housing is oriented on your specific engine bay layout.

### Removal
1. Disconnect the oil pressure/level sensor connectors if they're mounted on the housing.
2. Remove the housing mounting bolts, noting their positions, they're not all identical length on some versions.
3. Lift the housing away from the block, have a drain pan ready, there's always residual oil that comes with it.
4. Clean the mating surface on the block thoroughly.

### Installation
1. Install the new housing with a new gasket/seal, torque the mounting bolts evenly in a crisscross pattern.
2. Reconnect sensors and reinstall anything removed for access, refill with oil and a new filter element, check for leaks once running.
entries.torque_specs: Housing mounting bolts: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact engine revision, this varies by whether your housing uses a separate gasket or an integrated seal design.
entries.part_numbers: Oil filter housing assembly and mounting gasket/seal: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, there have been revised versions of this housing across the production run addressing earlier cracking issues, worth checking if a superseded part number applies to your car.
entries.tools_needed: Standard socket set, drain pan, possibly extensions/universal joints depending on access clearance.
entries.time_estimate: 2-3 hours depending on what needs to come off for access
entries.notes_warnings: If you're replacing the housing because the old one cracked, inspect it once it's out, cracking at the same spot repeatedly across many owners' cars is a known pattern on this engine family and is worth researching before you reinstall the exact same design if a revised part number exists. Don't skip cleaning the mating surface, a rushed cleanup here is the most common reason for a comeback leak.

entries.summary: Flush and replace the hydraulic power steering fluid. Old fluid turns dark and abrasive and is hard on the pump and rack seals.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Engine off and cool. Jack the front of the car and support it on stands so the wheels are off the ground, you'll need to turn the steering freely.
2. Place a drain pan under the reservoir area and lay rags down, this job makes a mess no matter how careful you are.

### Draining
1. Siphon as much old fluid out of the reservoir as you can with a turkey baster or fluid extractor.
2. For a more complete flush, disconnect the return line into a drain pan and cap the reservoir outlet so it doesn't siphon the new fluid straight back out.
3. With the return line draining, have someone turn the steering lock to lock slowly while you keep topping the reservoir up, never let it run dry or you'll pump air into the system.

### Refilling and bleeding
1. Reconnect the return line and fill the reservoir with the correct spec fluid.
2. With the engine off and wheels off the ground, turn the steering slowly lock to lock several times to work air out, topping up as the level drops.
3. Start the engine briefly and repeat the lock-to-lock cycles, checking the level each time.
4. Lower the car, check for leaks at the return line connection, and check the level once the system is at operating temperature.
entries.torque_specs: Return line clamp or fitting: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec. These are low-torque fittings, overtightening a hose clamp here damages the hose.
entries.part_numbers: Power steering fluid: BMW specifies a particular fluid for this system (commonly a CHF-type hydraulic fluid rather than conventional ATF on this generation), verify the correct spec against your owner's manual or RealOEM.com before buying. Using the wrong fluid attacks the seals.
entries.tools_needed: Fluid extractor or turkey baster, drain pan, jack and stands, plenty of rags, a second person helps a lot for the lock-to-lock cycling.
entries.notes_warnings: Never let the reservoir run dry while cycling the steering, that pumps air deep into the system and turns a simple fluid change into a long bleeding session. Whining from the pump after the job almost always means trapped air, not a failed pump, cycle it again before assuming the worst. Use only the BMW-specified fluid, this is one of those places where generic is actively harmful rather than just suboptimal.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the rear shock absorbers. On this chassis the rear spring and shock are separate components, which makes this a notably easier and safer job than the front struts.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the rear wheel bolts, jack the car, support it on stands, remove the wheel.
2. Support the rear trailing arm with a jack so the suspension stays loaded as you work.

### Removal
1. Access the upper shock mount. Depending on body style this may mean pulling back trim in the trunk or under the parcel shelf to reach the top nut.
2. Remove the lower shock bolt at the trailing arm.
3. Remove the upper mount nut and withdraw the shock. The mount hardware and dust boot usually come out with it.

### Installation
1. Fit the new shock with a new mount and bump stop, same reasoning as the front, these are wear items and cheap relative to doing the job twice.
2. Start the upper nut and the lower bolt by hand before torquing either.
3. Torque the lower bolt with the suspension at ride height, not hanging free, so the bushing isn't preloaded into a permanently twisted position.
4. Refit any trim removed for access, reinstall the wheel, lower the car.
entries.torque_specs: Upper shock mount nut and lower shock bolt: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, and check whether yours are one-time-use before planning to reuse them.
entries.part_numbers: Rear shocks, upper mounts, and bump stops: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Sport suspension and standard are different part numbers.
entries.tools_needed: Torque wrench, jack and stands, trim removal tools for the upper mount access, penetrating fluid.
entries.notes_warnings: Much less dangerous than the front struts since the spring stays in the car, no spring compressor needed. Replace in pairs across the axle. If you're also doing the rear trailing arm bushings, do both jobs in the same session, the teardown overlaps significantly.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the rear trailing arm bushings, a well-known wear point on this chassis. Worn RTABs show up as rear-end vagueness, a slight steering sensation from the back of the car under throttle or braking, and uneven rear tyre wear.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the rear wheel bolts, jack the car, support it on stands, remove the wheel.
2. Support the trailing arm with a jack, you'll need to control its position throughout.
3. Soak the bushing bracket bolts in penetrating fluid.

### Removal
1. Remove the bolts holding the trailing arm bushing bracket to the body.
2. Lower the trailing arm just enough to access the bushing, without stretching the brake line or ABS wire, disconnect their brackets if needed rather than straining them.
3. Press the old bushing out. This genuinely needs an RTAB removal/installation tool kit, the bushing is a tight interference fit and improvising here usually damages the arm.

### Installation
1. Press the new bushing in with the tool, paying attention to orientation. These bushings are directional and installing one rotated incorrectly ruins its intended compliance.
2. Reattach the bracket to the body, hand-start the bolts.
3. Final-torque with the suspension at ride height, not drooping on the jack. This matters more here than almost anywhere else on the car, a bushing torqued at full droop is permanently preloaded and will tear.
4. Reinstall the wheel, lower the car, get a rear alignment.
entries.torque_specs: Trailing arm bushing bracket bolts: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, and check whether they're one-time-use before planning to reuse them.
entries.part_numbers: RTAB bushings, and the limiter kit if you choose to fit one: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. There are also polyurethane and solid monoball aftermarket options, each trading compliance and noise for precision, worth researching before committing since they feel very different on the road.
entries.tools_needed: RTAB removal and installation tool kit (rentable from many parts stores), torque wrench, jack and stands, penetrating fluid.
entries.time_estimate: 2-4 hours per side depending on corrosion
entries.notes_warnings: Bushing orientation is the step people get wrong, check the alignment marks before pressing. Doing this job is a natural time to also do rear shocks since the teardown overlaps. Get a rear alignment afterward, this directly affects rear toe.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the accessory belt that drives the alternator, water pump, power steering pump, and AC compressor off the front of the engine.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Note the belt routing before removing anything, either photograph it or check the routing diagram sticker under the hood, you'll need it to install the new one correctly.

### Removal
1. Use a breaker bar or a dedicated tensioner tool on the tensioner pulley to release belt tension.
2. Slip the belt off the pulleys, starting with whichever is easiest to reach.
3. While it's off, spin the tensioner and idler pulleys by hand, feel for roughness or play, replace them if anything feels off, they're cheap compared to a belt failure later.

### Installation
1. Route the new belt exactly per the diagram, the last pulley you route it onto is usually the alternator or AC compressor.
2. Release the tensioner slowly and confirm the belt has seated properly in every pulley groove before starting the engine.
entries.torque_specs: Tensioner pulley mounting bolt: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact engine revision before relying on a memorized number, this is not a high-stakes fastener in terms of failure mode but it's still worth getting right.
entries.part_numbers: Serpentine belt and tensioner/idler pulleys: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, there are revisions across the production run of this engine.
entries.tools_needed: Tensioner release tool or a long breaker bar, flashlight to see the routing clearly.
entries.notes_warnings: A mis-routed belt can spin the AC compressor or alternator backward, which is not something you want to discover after you've already started the engine. Double check the routing diagram before you pull the old belt off, not after.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace worn anti-roll bar (sway bar) end links. Usually the cause of a light rattle or knock over small bumps that sounds much worse than the actual repair is.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the wheel bolts, jack the car, support it on stands, remove the wheel.
2. Soak both end link nuts in penetrating fluid, these seize more often than almost anything else on the car.

### Removal
1. Hold the ball stud still while you undo the nut. Most end links have a hex or torx socket in the end of the stud exactly for this, otherwise the whole stud just spins and you'll be there a while.
2. Remove the upper nut (strut or subframe end) and the lower nut (sway bar end).
3. Withdraw the old link. If the stud spins hopelessly and won't come off, cutting the link is a legitimate last resort since it's being replaced anyway.

### Installation
1. Fit the new link, start both nuts by hand.
2. Torque both ends to spec, holding the stud still the same way you did on removal.
3. Reinstall the wheel and lower the car.
entries.torque_specs: End link nuts: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec. These are modest fasteners, overtightening damages the ball joint boot and the new link will fail early.
entries.part_numbers: Sway bar end links, front and rear: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Front and rear are different lengths, and some years differ between standard and sport suspension.
entries.tools_needed: Penetrating fluid, torque wrench, and whatever hex or torx bit fits the counter-hold in your link's stud, check before you start so you're not stuck mid-job.
entries.notes_warnings: Among the cheapest fixes for a suspension noise, always worth ruling out before chasing more expensive parts. Replace both sides at once, they wear at the same rate and you've already got the car up. No alignment needed afterward, end links don't affect geometry.

entries.summary: Replace worn outer tie rod ends. Symptoms are play in the steering, a knock when turning at low speed, and uneven inner or outer tyre wear.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Loosen the wheel bolts, jack the car, support it on stands, remove the front wheel.
2. Before loosening anything, mark the position of the outer tie rod on its threaded shaft, or count the exact number of turns as you remove it. This gets you close to the original toe setting and makes the car safe to drive to the alignment shop.
3. Soak the ball joint nut and the lock nut in penetrating fluid.

### Removal
1. Loosen the lock nut that holds the outer tie rod against the inner rod.
2. Remove the castle nut or locking nut at the steering knuckle.
3. Separate the ball joint with a proper separator tool, not by hammering the knuckle.
4. Unscrew the outer tie rod off the inner rod, counting turns as you go.

### Installation
1. Thread the new outer tie rod on the same number of turns you counted, to land close to the original toe.
2. Insert the ball joint into the knuckle and torque its nut to spec, fitting a new cotter pin if your design uses one.
3. Snug the lock nut against the outer tie rod, but leave the final tightening to after alignment if the shop prefers to set it themselves.
4. Reinstall the wheel, lower the car.
5. Get a four-wheel alignment. This is not optional on a steering component, counting turns gets you drivable, not correct.
entries.torque_specs: Tie rod ball joint nut and lock nut: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec. If your design uses a cotter pin, never reuse the old one.
entries.part_numbers: Outer tie rod ends, and inner tie rods if those are also worn: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Left and right can differ.
entries.tools_needed: Ball joint separator, torque wrench, penetrating fluid, jack and stands.
entries.notes_warnings: Check the inner tie rods while you're in there, grab the inner rod and feel for play, there's no point replacing only the outer if the inner is also worn. Counting threads on removal is the single trick that makes this job go smoothly, skip it and you're guessing at toe. Alignment afterward is mandatory, this is a steering component and getting it wrong affects how the car tracks and brakes.

entries.summary: Replace a leaking valve cover gasket, a common age-related leak on this engine, usually shows up as a faint burning smell or visible seepage down the back of the engine.
entries.steps:
### Preparation
1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal.

### Removal
1. Remove the engine cover and intake components in the way, on this engine that typically includes some combination of the ignition coil connectors, coil packs themselves, and nearby wiring harness clips.
2. Disconnect the VANOS solenoid connectors near the front of the cover if they're in the way of cover removal.
3. Remove the valve cover bolts in the reverse of the tightening sequence below, lift the cover off carefully, the gasket is often integrated into the cover itself on this engine rather than a separate piece.
4. Clean the cylinder head mating surface thoroughly, any old gasket material or oil residue left behind causes a new leak almost immediately.

### Installation
1. Install the new cover/gasket, hand-thread all bolts first before torquing any of them.
2. Torque bolts in a crisscross pattern working from the center bolts outward, in stages rather than going straight to full torque on each bolt.
3. Reconnect everything in reverse, reconnect the battery, start the engine and check for leaks after it's warmed up.
entries.torque_specs: This engine was built with two different valve cover designs across its production run, a plastic cover and a magnesium/aluminum cover, and they have different specs. Plastic cover bolts: commonly cited around 9 Nm. Magnesium cover bolts: commonly cited around 7 Nm plus an additional 90 degree turn, and those bolts are typically a one-time-use, torque-to-yield design, don't reuse them. Confirm which cover type you actually have before using either number, and verify against RealOEM or dealer spec regardless.
entries.part_numbers: Valve cover (with integrated gasket, if your design uses one) and cover bolts if they're the one-time-use type: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, this is one of the areas where getting the wrong variant for your specific cover type is an easy mistake.
entries.tools_needed: Torque wrench capable of low Nm values and angle-based tightening if your cover uses the torque-to-yield bolts, basic hand tools for the intake/coil components in the way.
entries.time_estimate: 1.5-2.5 hours depending on what's in the way on your specific car
entries.notes_warnings: Identify your cover type (plastic vs magnesium/aluminum) before you start, the wrong torque spec on the wrong bolt type either leaves it loose enough to leak immediately or over-torques a one-time-use bolt. Never reuse torque-to-yield bolts if that's what your cover uses. Take photos of connector routing before you start disconnecting things, there are more clips and connectors in this area than you'll remember afterward.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, cross-checked against public forum and retailer-guide discussion of this specific job (BMW enthusiast forums, Pelican Parts' public E90 tech article index). Not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, and confirm your actual cover type before relying on either torque figure.
